analysis.one_liner: Repeals Obamacare's insurance rules and lets insurers sell plans nationwide under the loosest state's rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it died without ever receiving a vote or a hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the entire first title of the Affordable Care Act—the part requiring insurers to cover people with pre-existing conditions, cover a standard set of benefits, and price plans the same for sick and healthy people [S2, S3]. It would then let a health insurer pick one state as its "primary state" and sell individual insurance in every other state under that state's rules, exempting the insurer from most laws of the states where its customers actually live [S3]. The buyer's own state could not regulate the plan; only the insurer's chosen state could enforce the rules [S3]. The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote [S5, S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers selling individual-market coverage would gain the most: they could designate a single permissive state as their regulator, escape benefit mandates and rate rules in every state where they sell, and market thinner, cheaper plans to healthy customers. Some healthy, higher-income buyers might find lower premiums. The bill would also benefit people who prefer minimal coverage they can buy cheaply.

how_it_helps.text: It would let insurers sell individual plans nationwide under the rules of one state they choose, avoiding the mandates, rate restrictions, and consumer protections of every other state, which could lower premiums for some buyers.

It would roll back ACA requirements that insurers cover essential benefits, charge community rates, and accept applicants with pre-existing conditions, freeing insurers to underwrite and design bare-bones policies.

It did include some consumer guardrails: insurers had to disclose prominently that the policy may not cover services the buyer's state mandates, could not re-rate an individual at renewal for health status, had to meet risk-based capital standards, and had to offer independent external review of denied claims [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions and those who need comprehensive coverage would bear the cost: as insurers sell leaner plans nationwide under the loosest rules, sicker and older customers would be left in a shrinking, more expensive pool. States would also lose regulatory power over plans sold to their own residents.

drawbacks.text: Selling across state lines under the primary state's laws would let insurers offer plans that skip benefits a buyer's own state requires and avoid that state's rate protections; the bill's own mandatory disclosure tells purchasers the policy 'may be less expensive than others because it is not subject to all of the insurance laws' of their state [S3].

Repealing ACA title I rolls back federal protections for people with pre-existing conditions in the individual market; the bill orders a GAO study of the effect on coverage and cost for people with pre-existing conditions, an acknowledgment that those effects were the central risk [S3, S2].

State regulators would lose much of their power over plans sold into their states: enforcement of most consumer rules would sit with the insurer's chosen primary state, with the secondary state limited to a short list of financial-solvency, fraud, and claims-practice actions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill might have lowered premiums for some healthy buyers, and it did carry some safeguards—required financial examinations, solvency-based capital, independent external appeal of claim denials, a ban on re-rating an individual for health status at renewal, and a mandated disclosure that the policy skips the buyer's state's mandates and rate protections [S3]. But the core trade is repealing the ACA's individual-market protections—including community rating and guaranteed issue—and letting insurers sell under the loosest state's rules, which most health economists and state regulators predicted would split the market: cheap skimpy plans for healthy people and rapidly escalating, less available coverage for anyone sick. The bill also imposed onerous disclosure requirements and some federal conditions on insurers, but the cost side for consumers dominated [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Ted Cruz introduced the bill on October 26, 2017, with Marco Rubio as the only cosponsor; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5, S1].
No further action was ever taken—the bill never left the Finance Committee and received no vote in the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who depend on the ACA's individual-market protections kept them, since nothing changed; the bill's insurer-facing provisions never took effect either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients and ACA protections kept intact

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole lead sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it—notably, its chairman (Sen. Orrin Hatch, R-UT) never scheduled a markup or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsor and cosponsor were Republicans; with only two Republicans attached and no Democratic support, the bill never advanced, and repeal of the ACA's consumer protections had already failed on the Senate floor earlier in 2017 (a widely reported 49-51 vote in July 2017).

industries.note: The bill frees insurers to shop for the most permissive state regulator, sell thinner plans nationwide, and escape state coverage mandates and rate rules, while keeping the protections they must honor to a short list they help define. Some of the resulting cheaper plans would be sold directly to consumers.

States would lose the authority to regulate plans sold to their own residents by out-of-state insurers, keeping only financial-solvency checks, fraud enforcement, and limited claims-practice authority. Consumers lose a layer of local protection.

industries.industry: People with pre-existing conditions and enrollees in ACA-compliant plans
industries.note: Repealing ACA title I ends guaranteed issue, essential benefits, and community rating; healthier buyers might find cheaper plans, while people with health conditions would face the pre-ACA dynamics of medical underwriting, though the bill bans re-rating an individual at renewal for health status.
